title: Reduced closed orbits for a stabilizer-preserving etale groupoid map
statement: Let $S$ be a scheme [def-pc-scheme], and let $F:(U\prime,R\prime,s\prime,t\prime,e\prime,i\prime,c\prime)\to(U,R,s,t,e,i,c)$ be a morphism of groupoid schemes over $S$ [def-a1-scheme-groupoid-laws], with object and arrow maps $a,b$. Suppose $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$, $R=\operatorname{Spec}B$, $U\prime=\operatorname{Spec}A\prime$, $R\prime=\operatorname{Spec}B\prime$ are affine [def-weil-affine-spectrum], all four source and target maps are finite locally free [def-pc-finite-locally-free], and $a$ is etale [def-weil-etale-morphism]. Write $G=R\times_{(s,t),U\times_SU,\Delta_U}U$ and $G\prime=R\prime\times_{(s\prime,t\prime),U\prime\times_SU\prime,\Delta_{U\prime}}U\prime$ [def-pc-fibre-product]. Assume the source square, target square, and stabilizer square $(G\prime\to G,U\prime\to U)$ are cartesian. Put $C=\{x\in A:s^*x=t^*x\}$ and $C\prime=\{x\in A\prime:(s\prime)^*x=(t\prime)^*x\}$. Assume $C$ is a strictly henselian local ring [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology], with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, and let $p\prime\in\operatorname{Spec}C\prime$ lie above $\mathfrak m$. Let $Z\subset U$ and $Z\prime\subset U\prime$ be the sets of points over $\mathfrak m$ and $p\prime$, respectively. Then $Z,Z\prime$ are nonempty finite sets of closed points, $a:Z\prime\to Z$ is a bijection, and $\kappa(a(u\prime))\to\kappa(u\prime)$ is an isomorphism for every $u\prime\in Z\prime$. Here residue fields use [def-weil-residue-field]. If $J=\sqrt{\mathfrak m A}$ and $J\prime=\bigcap_{u\prime\in Z\prime}u\prime\subset A\prime$ (points being regarded as prime ideals), the induced homomorphism $A/J\to A\prime/J\prime$ is an isomorphism.

source.place: Tag 0DT9 (lemma-etale), proof of the claim, first part: from "Observe that U_p and U\prime_{p\prime} have finitely many points" through the definition of J\prime; reduced coordinate rings by finite Chinese remainder. proof.text: The morphism of groupoids carries invariant functions to invariant functions: for $c\in C$, $(s\prime)^*a^*c=b^*s^*c=b^*t^*c=(t\prime)^*a^*c$. Thus $C\to C\prime$ and the maps of invariant spectra commute. Apply [lem-a1-affine-groupoid-integral-invariants] to both affine groupoids: $C\subset A$ and $C\prime\subset A\prime$ are integral. Apply [lem-a1-affine-groupoid-orbit-fibres] to both: $Z,Z\prime$ are nonempty single ordinary-point orbits, and $a(Z\prime)\subset Z$. For any point $w$ of either orbit, that orbit equals the target image of the source fibre over $w$. These source fibres have finitely many points by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-closed-map-finite-fibres], since finite locally free maps are finite by [def-pc-finite-locally-free]. Consequently both $Z$ and $Z\prime$ are finite.

source.place: Tag 0DT9 (groupoids-lemma-etale), first part of the strictly henselian claim

proof.text: Put $k=C/\mathfrak m=\kappa(\mathfrak m)$. It is separably closed by [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology]. For each $u\in Z$, [lem-a1-integral-residue-extension-algebraic] applied to $C\subset A$ makes $\kappa(u)/k$ algebraic. By [lem-sfb-algebraic-sepclosed-purely-insep], $\kappa(u)$ is separably closed and $\kappa(u)/k$ is purely inseparable. For $u\prime\in Z\prime$ above $u$, apply [lem-exc-etale-lift-sepclosed-base] to $a$, $L=\kappa(u)$, $\Omega=\kappa(u\prime)$, the residue embedding $\beta:L\to\Omega$, and the canonical residue points $\tau:\operatorname{Spec}L\to U$, $g:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to U\prime$. It gives $g\prime:\operatorname{Spec}L\to U\prime$ with $g\prime\operatorname{Spec}\beta=g$ and $ag\prime=\tau$. Its image is $u\prime$. Taking the residue maps gives $\lambda:\kappa(u\prime)\to L$ with $\lambda\beta=1_L$ and $\beta\lambda=1_\Omega$. Hence the original residue map $\beta$ is an isomorphism.

source.place: Tag 0DT9 (groupoids-lemma-etale), first part of the strictly henselian claim

proof.text: Choose $u\prime\in Z\prime$ and put $u=a(u\prime)$. The cartesian source square gives $R\prime\times_{U\prime}\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(u\prime)\cong R\times_U\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(u\prime)$. By step 2 this is the original source fibre $R\times_U\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(u)$. Given $v\in Z$, [lem-a1-affine-groupoid-orbit-fibres] supplies a point $r\in R$ with $s(r)=u,t(r)=v$. Use the canonical $\kappa(r)$-point of $R$ and the $\kappa(r)$-point of $U\prime$ obtained from $\kappa(u\prime)\cong\kappa(u)\to\kappa(r)$ to lift to a $\kappa(r)$-point of $R\prime$. Its source is $u\prime$; its target $v\prime$ lies above $v$. Source and target agree on every invariant in $C\prime$, so $v\prime$ has the same image $p\prime$ as $u\prime$ in $\operatorname{Spec}C\prime$. Thus $v\prime\in Z\prime$ and $a:Z\prime\to Z$ is surjective.

source.place: Tag 0DT9 (groupoids-lemma-etale), first part of the strictly henselian claim

proof.text: Let $u\prime_1,u\prime_2\in Z\prime$ have the same image $u$. By [lem-a1-affine-groupoid-orbit-fibres], choose $r\prime\in R\prime$ with endpoints $u\prime_1,u\prime_2$. Set $H=\kappa(r\prime)$. The two endpoint maps $\kappa(u)\to H$ agree on $k$, because the invariant functions $C\to C\prime\to B\prime$ agree through source and target. They coincide: in characteristic $p>0$, each $x\in\kappa(u)$ has $x^{p^n}\in k$ by step 2, so their images have the same $p^n$-th power and hence are equal in the field $H$; in characteristic zero $\kappa(u)=k$. Therefore the canonical $H$-point of $R\prime$ has image in $R$ whose source and target are the same $H$-point of $U$, not merely the same underlying point. The definition of $G$ as the diagonal fibre product gives an $H$-point of $G$. Pair it with the source $H$-point in $U\prime$. The cartesian stabilizer square gives an $H$-point of $G\prime$. Its image in $R\prime$ equals the original $H$-point: both have the same image in $R$ and the same source in $U\prime$, and the source square is cartesian. In $G\prime$ the two endpoints coincide, so $u\prime_1=u\prime_2$. This proves injectivity.

source.place: Tag 0DT9 (groupoids-lemma-etale), first part of the strictly henselian claim

proof.text: Every point $q$ of $Z$ is closed in $\operatorname{Spec}A$, and every point $q\prime$ of $Z\prime$ is closed in $\operatorname{Spec}A\prime$, by the following elementary argument (the proof of Stacks Tag 00GA, algebra-lemma-finite-residue-extension-closed). Both $A/q$ and $A\prime/q\prime$ contain $k=C/\mathfrak m$, because these primes contract to $\mathfrak m$ in $C$. They embed into their residue fields, which are algebraic over $k$ by step 2. If $0\ne x$ lies in either domain, an algebraic equation $c_0+c_1x+\cdots+c_nx^n=0$ can be chosen with $c_0\ne0$ by cancelling powers of $x$. It gives $x^{-1}=-c_0^{-1}(c_1+\cdots+c_nx^{n-1})$ in that domain. Thus both quotients are fields and the primes are maximal. The finite sets $Z,Z\prime$ are consequently closed subsets of their ambient affine schemes.

source.place: Tag 00GA (algebra-lemma-finite-residue-extension-closed), proof, with the inverse polynomial written out

proof.text: The prime ideals containing $\mathfrak mA$ are exactly $Z$, since their contractions contain the maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ and are proper. Thus [lem-weil-pbc-zero-locus-eq-iff-radical-eq] gives $J=\bigcap_{q\in Z}q$. Distinct maximal ideals are coprime: if $q+q_1$ were proper, maximality of $q$ would give $q_1\subset q$ and then $q=q_1$. Apply [lem-pc-crt-ideal-quotient-product] to the finite sets of maximal ideals $Z$ and $Z\prime$. Since $A/q=\kappa(q)$ and $A\prime/q\prime=\kappa(q\prime)$ for maximal ideals, it gives $A/J\cong\prod_{q\in Z}\kappa(q)$ and $A\prime/J\prime\cong\prod_{q\prime\in Z\prime}\kappa(q\prime)$. The map $a^*$ sends $J$ into $J\prime$: each $q\prime$ pulls back to its image $q\in Z$. On these products its $q\prime$-coordinate is precisely $\kappa(a(q\prime))\to\kappa(q\prime)$, since reducing $a^*f$ at $q\prime$ is the residue of $f$ at $a(q\prime)$ followed by the residue map. Steps 2-4 make this a product of isomorphisms indexed by a bijection. Its inverse takes each coordinate back through the inverse residue map and the inverse index bijection. This proves that the induced $A/J\to A\prime/J\prime$ is an isomorphism.
